structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland resident families with children under age 13 (or individuals ages 13–19 with a qualifying disability) who are working, in an approved training program, or attending school, and whose income meets CCS guidelines. Also eligible: recipients of Temporary Cash Assistance (TCA), Supplemental Security Income (SSI), or TANF. Families experiencing homelessness and Head Start referrals are also served. Migrant workers, minor parents, and families participating in the Montgomery County Guaranteed Basic Income Program may also qualify. Both families and licensed/registered child care providers are program participants.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Payment for child care services provided by Maryland licensed child care centers, registered family child care homes, informal relative care providers, or non-relative care in the child's home. Scholarships can also be used for before and after school child care and extended day services for Head Start enrollees. Care cannot commence before MSDE approval is received for informal providers.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide across Maryland for families who are Maryland residents. Informal child care arrangements must be approved by the Maryland State Department of Education before care begins. Non-relative informal care can only be provided within the child's home; relative informal care can be provided in the child's home or provider's home.
requirements_list: Must be a Maryland resident
Must be working/employed, in an approved training program, or attending school (for households where both parents live together, both must meet all eligibility requirements)

Must be a recipient of Temporary Cash Assistance (TCA), Supplemental Security Income (SSI), or TANF, OR have family income below CCS income guidelines (varies by family size and application type; initial income scale maximum for family of 2 is $76,117; continuation income scale maximum for family of 2 is $86,266)

Child must be under age 13, or an individual ages 13–19 with a qualifying disability (defined as being physically or mentally incapable of self-care appropriate to age, verified by physician, licensed/certified psychologist, or licensed social worker)
Child must be a U.S. citizen or qualified alien with documentation (birth certificate or citizenship status documentation required); parents are NOT required to be U.S. citizens
All household members must provide proof of identity (valid unexpired U.S. passport, birth certificate, valid driver's license, or current photo ID)
Head of household must provide a Photo ID
Child must be immunized to Maryland state standards or documentation supporting exemption must be provided
Must provide proof of employment or enrollment in training/school
Must provide proof of residency (utility bill, lease, rental agreement, mortgage statement, or unexpired Maryland driver's license with current address)

Must provide proof of income (most recent four weeks of consecutive pay stubs for standard employment; previous year tax return if after April 15 or profit/loss statements for past 3 months if before April 15 for self-employment)
Must register in and use the Child Care Scholarship Family Portal at https://family.childcareportals.org
Must complete recertification/renewal process on time to maintain scholarship
Families referred through DHS (Department of Human Services), Head Start, or with homelessness status may qualify through special referral pathways
Families receiving TANF, TCA, or SSI are exempt from the enrollment freeze and can receive scholarships immediately upon approval
Existing enrolled families may add new children to their scholarship without being subject to the enrollment freeze
Must be willing and able to provide documentation of all required eligibility criteria before determination can be made

For informal provider care: provider must complete criminal background check (fingerprinting), child protective services background check (notarized consent), health & safety training (3-hour Basic training plus 1.5-hour Annual Update), CPR and First Aid certification (in-person skills training required, American Heart Association or equivalent), emergency preparedness plan, emergency care & medication authorization form, proof of residency, proof of identity, proof of SSN/ITIN for payment eligibility, and pass care location inspection

For informal relative care: must provide proof of relatedness (birth certificate, marriage license, passport, insurance policy, religious record, adoption papers, or other legal documentation) if provider is great-grandparent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, or older sibling; relatedness documentation not required for other kinship relationships (great-aunt/uncle, cousin, etc.)

For informal care of non-school-age children: must provide current MDH Immunization Certificate (MDH 896 or equivalent) and blood-lead testing certificate (MDH 4620 or equivalent) for children under 6 years old
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Step 1: Create an account in the Child Care Scholarship Family Portal at https://family.childcareportals.org. Complete the required fields including name, date of birth, email, and phone number. Verify email with sent code. Step 2: For first-time applicants, submit a Fast Track scholarship application online (3 business day processing). Upload three required documents: (1) proof of employment or training/school enrollment, (2) proof of residency (utility bill, lease, or Maryland driver's license showing current address), and (3) proof of income (most recent 4 weeks of pay stubs for employment, employment verification form for new jobs, or proof of TCA/SSI). Step 3: Fast Track application is processed within three business days by CCS Central 2. Step 4: If eligible, a temporary 60-day Fast Track scholarship is issued. Step 5: Within 15 days of submitting the Fast Track application, submit additional documents for full 52-week scholarship evaluation: most recent four weeks of consecutive pay stubs, proof of identity for all household members (government-issued photo ID for adults; birth certificate for children), proof of approved activity on employer or school letterhead, proof of all other income sources, proof of address (utility bill, lease, rental or mortgage agreement, or driver's license), and proof of citizenship/qualified alien status for all children (U.S. birth certificate or Head Start enrollment proof). Step 6: If all documents are provided within 15 days, eligibility for the 52-week scholarship is determined before the temporary scholarship expires. If not provided within 15 days, a Missing Information Letter is sent. Step 7: Families subject to the enrollment freeze will be placed on a waitlist and issued scholarships when the freeze is lifted, unless they are TANF, TCA, or SSI recipients who can receive scholarships immediately upon approval. Step 8: Once scholarship is approved and issued, family selects a participating child care provider. Step 9: Provider accepts or denies scholarship request (5 business days to respond). Step 10: Once provider accepts, child begins care and provider submits invoices for reimbursement. Changes to existing scholarships can be reported through the Family Child Care Portal using interim change forms (Change of Address, Change of Circumstance, Change of Provider, Child Turning 13, etc.). Redetermination applications must be submitted 45 days before eligibility end date. Applicants can call CCS Central 2 at 877-227-0125 (press 3) for assistance completing their application. Interpreter services are available in multiple languages.

structured_extraction.program_name: Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP)
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides nutritionally balanced meals and snacks to eligible children and adults in participating childcare and daycare settings. Eligible participants include young children (including infants) in childcare centers, daycare homes, afterschool care programs, and emergency shelters, as well as adults over 60 or living with disabilities enrolled in adult daycare facilities. Meals meet USDA nutrition standards and contribute to healthy growth, development, and wellness. Over 300 agencies across Maryland participate, and funds help offset meal and snack costs for public, private nonprofit, and proprietary centers licensed to provide non-residential childcare or adult daycare services.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: CACFP reimburses participating child and adult care agencies with federally-funded dollars for meals and snacks that comply with USDA nutrition standards and meal patterns. The annual maximum reimbursement for a child or adult care center serving 25 free-eligible participants breakfast, lunch, and a snack 5 days per week varies. The annual maximum reimbursement for a family child care home serving 6 Tier I participants breakfast, lunch, and a snack 5 days per week also varies. Sponsors receive cash-in-lieu of USDA Foods with their meal reimbursements. Emergency shelters receive meal reimbursement at the highest rates with minimal paperwork requirements. Providers manage financial claims through the Maryland Accountability and Reporting System (MARS). Applications are processed annually.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Childcare centers, daycare homes, afterschool care programs, emergency shelters serving children, adult daycare facilities serving older adults (60+) and adults with disabilities, including public, private nonprofit, and for-profit licensed providers
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Meals and snacks that meet USDA nutrition standards and meal patterns for participating agencies; funds offset meal and supplement costs for licensed non-residential child and adult care providers. Centers can also earn Core of Knowledge hours and increase their EXCELS rating level through participation.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide throughout all Maryland counties. Family Child Care Providers participate through specific sponsoring organizations serving different regions of the state: Cecil County Government serves Cecil, Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Harford, and Kent counties; Frederick County Community Action Agency serves Frederick and Carroll counties; Montgomery County Public Schools serves Montgomery County; Prince George's County Public Schools serves Prince George's County; and The Planning Council serves all counties. Over 300 agencies participate across the state.
requirements_list: Must be licensed to provide non-residential child or adult care services
Agencies must comply with USDA nutrition standards and meal patterns
For emergency shelters, children 18 years and younger are automatically eligible for free meals with no family application forms required
Family Child Care Providers must work through designated sponsoring agencies
For adults: must be 60 or older, or living with a disability
Centers must complete CACFP Basics Training and three-part online application
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: For Child and Adult Care Centers: (1) Call MSDE at (410) 767-0199 to begin the CACFP Interest Process; (2) Complete the CACFP Interest Survey and Budget Worksheet; (3) MSDE determines eligibility; (4) Complete CACFP Basics Training and three-part online application; (5) MSDE completes a pre-approval visit; (6) MSDE approves the center to participate in CACFP and the center can begin claiming reimbursement. For Family Child Care Homes: Contact your designated sponsoring organization based on your location (Cecil County Government, Frederick County Community Action Agency, Montgomery County Public Schools, Prince George's County Public Schools, or The Planning Council). Providers manage financial claims through the Maryland Accountability and Reporting System (MARS).

structured_extraction.program_description: A federal grant program that requires local education agencies identified as having significant racial or ethnic disproportionality in special education identification, placement, or discipline to reserve 15 percent of IDEA Part B Section 611 and Section 619 funds to implement proactive and responsive actions addressing root causes of these disparities. The program funds educational and behavioral evaluations, services, support, professional development, and systemic organizational change efforts to reduce overidentification and promote equity.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Local education agencies identified by the State as having data indicating over-identification must reserve 15 percent of IDEA Part B Section 611 and Section 619 funds to implement comprehensive systems addressing root causes of disproportionality. Funds support: educational and behavioral evaluations, services, and support including evidence-based literacy instruction; professional development and staff training; coaching and consultation; data systems supporting decision-making; progress monitoring; implementation evaluation; and systemic organizational change efforts. Allowable costs include coaches/mentors, extended contracts/hours, general education teacher salaries for interventions and assessments, guidance counselor and school-based psychologist salaries for behavioral interventions and evaluations, RTI/MTSS coordinator salaries, school social worker salaries, substitute teacher salaries, travel for professional development, tutoring services, computing devices for intervention delivery, instructional materials and software exclusively for interventions. Funds may not be used for: special education eligibility evaluations, occupational/physical therapy services, universal screening, core curriculum, student transportation, office equipment, rent/occupancy costs, or furniture.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Identified LEAs must submit comprehensive plans; interim progress reports due January 31, final reports due November 30 annually
structured_extraction.contact_name: Gary W. Richardson, MBA (Branch Chief, Resource Management and Monitoring) and Demetria White (Interagency Specialist)
structured_extraction.program_audience: Local education agencies (LEAs) identified as having significant disproportionality in special education identification, placement, or discipline based on race or ethnicity over two or more consecutive years.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Educational and behavioral evaluations, services, and support including evidence-based literacy instruction; professional development; staff training and coaching; consultation; data systems supporting decision making; progress monitoring; implementation evaluation; and systemic organizational change efforts to address root causes of disproportionality. Funds must be used to identify and address factors contributing to significant disproportionality, which may include lack of access to scientifically-based instruction, economic/cultural/linguistic barriers to appropriate identification or placement, inappropriate use of disciplinary removals, lack of access to appropriate diagnostic screenings, differences in academic achievement levels, and policies/practices/procedures that contribute to disproportionality.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Maryland statewide. Applies to local education agencies identified by the State as having one or more student subgroups with a risk ratio greater than 2.0 for two or more consecutive years in identification, placement, or disciplinary actions (unless the risk ratio declines by defined amount).
requirements_list: Local education agency must be identified by the State as having significant disproportionality in identification based on race or ethnicity
Agency must have one or more subgroups of students with a risk ratio greater than 2.0 for two or more consecutive years (unless the risk ratio declines by defined amount)
Agency must reserve 15 percent of IDEA Part B Section 611 and Section 619 funds for CCEIS activities
Agency must use non-supplant funds (supplement, not replace, state/local/other federal funds)
Agency must address root cause factors contributing to significant disproportionality
Agency must address and review policies, practices, or procedures identified as contributing to overidentification
Agency must build systemic awareness and leadership supports
Agency must establish diverse stakeholder group (including families, general/special education staff, administrators, community members) for planning and co-implementation
Agency must conduct self-assessment and data review process
Agency must plan proactive and responsive actions to increase equity and decrease overidentification
Agency must develop comprehensive evaluation system for plan outcomes
Agency must conduct programmatic self-assessment using approved MSDE tool (IDEA Data Center Rubric, addressing root causes guide, or program review tool)
Agency must submit comprehensive CCEIS Plan including categories of analysis, root causes, planned response actions (PRAs), measurable goals, benchmarks, data sources, and detailed budgets
Agency must submit MSDE Grant Budget C-1-25 and Budget Detail Forms
Agency must submit interim progress reports (January 31) and final reports (November 30)
Agency must allow for plan amendments as needed
Identified LEAs receive annual review of policies, practices, and procedures
Identified LEAs must publicly report on revisions to policies, practices, and procedures
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Identified local education agencies submit comprehensive SFY 2025 CCEIS Plans following the state-provided template. The process includes: 1) Formation of local implementation team with diverse stakeholders responsible for co-development, data input, root cause analysis, co-implementation, and co-evaluation; 2) Review of categories of analysis data provided by the State in the Letter of Significant Disproportionality; 3) Completion of self-assessment and root cause analysis using MSDE-recommended tool (selecting from IDEA Data Center Equity Rubric, Addressing Root Causes guide, or WestEd Program Review Tool); 4) Identification of root cause factors for each area of significant disproportionality; 5) Development of Planned Response Actions (PRAs) for each identified root cause, including review/adjustment of policies/procedures/practices, academic/behavioral interventions, and professional learning; 6) Establishment of measurable outcomes with goals and interim benchmarks aligned to grant reporting periods; 7) Submission of detailed budget allocations by fund source (611 and/or 619); 8) Submission of supporting fiscal documents (C-1-25, Budget Detail Form); 9) Required signatures from local director of special education, chief academic officer, finance officer, superintendent, and MSDE liaisons. Implementation monitoring occurs through interim progress reports (January 31) tracking intervening supports provided, disability determinations, PRA progress, and budget expenditures. Plan amendments may be submitted throughout implementation using provided amendment template. Final progress and financial reports due November 30.

structured_extraction.program_description: A pre-employment program that provides counseling on post-secondary education options to Pre-ETS students with Autism, exposing them to various pathways such as apprenticeships, job training, direct job placement, and college.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Pre-ETS students with Autism participate in activities that introduce them to the education, training and employment options available to them after high school, including apprenticeships, career training, job placement, and college. Students participate in college tours and classroom activities designed to expose them to post-secondary education and career pathway options. The program also includes instruction in self-advocacy and social skills training to help develop soft skills needed to get and keep a job.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Pre-ETS students with documented Autism Spectrum Disorder diagnosis who are currently enrolled in high school, post-high school education program such as college, or another recognized educational program like a trade school, and are at least 14 years old but less than 22 years old.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Counseling and exposure to post-secondary education and career pathway options, including college tours, self-advocacy training, and social skills development.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available through DORS Pre-ETS programs in Maryland.
requirements_list: Be enrolled in Pre-ETS
Have a documented diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder

Be currently enrolled in high school (including home school or alternative secondary education program), a post-high school education program such as college, or another recognized educational program like a trade school
Be at least 14 years old but less than 22 years old
Have an Individualized Education Program (IEP), 504 plan, or medical records that document disability
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Eligible Pre-ETS students with Autism participate in classroom and other activities focused on exploring post-secondary education options and career pathways. Students should contact their DORS Counselor or local office for more information or request DORS Services.

structured_extraction.program_description: Consultation and support services to help people with disabilities explore, access, and participate in registered apprenticeship programs across Maryland. Services include assessments, academic instruction, exploration of apprenticeship opportunities, and ongoing support throughout the apprenticeship process.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: DORS provides multiple support services at no cost to eligible individuals with disabilities. Services include apprenticeship consultation to identify opportunities, academic assessment to determine current skill levels, in-depth exploration of various apprenticeship options, academic instruction to prepare for apprenticeships, pre-apprenticeship program support, registered apprenticeship program support, and youth apprenticeship tracking and support with transition assistance to registered apprenticeships. Registered apprenticeships are paid jobs where apprentices work on the job while receiving training from skilled craftspeople and related classroom instruction, with compensation according to a progressive pay scale.
structured_extraction.program_audience: People with disabilities in Maryland who are interested in pursuing registered apprenticeships.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Services support exploration, preparation, and participation in registered apprenticeship programs including academic assessment, instruction, and ongoing coordination throughout the apprenticeship.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available throughout the state of Maryland.
requirements_list: Must be a DORS consumer (individual receiving rehabilitation services from DORS)
Must be interested in exploring, accessing, or participating in registered apprenticeship programs
Must be 18 years of age
Must have a high school diploma (by means of high school graduation, GED, or NEDP)
Must be physically able to perform required tasks
Must be drug free
Must have transportation
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact Sam Grimsley, the Apprenticeship Coordinator, by phone at 410-554-9288 or email at Samantha.Grimsley@maryland.gov to discuss your interest in apprenticeships and the available consultation and support services. You can also visit occupations.mdapprenticeship.com to see a list of available apprenticeship occupations or call the statewide apprenticeship navigator at (410) 767-2246 or email info@mdapprenticeship.com for additional assistance in connecting with apprenticeship opportunities.

structured_extraction.program_description: A 16-week hands-on training course that prepares job seekers with disabilities for environmental service jobs in cleaning and facility maintenance.
list_of_eligible_industries: Administrative and Support and Waste Management and Remediation Services
list_of_relevant_industries: Administrative and Support and Waste Management and Remediation Services
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides 16 weeks of classroom and hands-on training at the Workforce & Technology Center campus in Baltimore. Training covers floor stripping, buffing, and waxing; dust mopping and damp mopping; trash collection; office, carpet, upholstery, and window cleaning; restroom cleaning; restocking supplies; and stairwell cleaning. Participants develop workplace skills needed for environmental service jobs. The program is designed for job seekers with disabilities to prepare them for employment in environmental services and facility maintenance positions.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Training and skills development for employment in environmental service positions.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Training is offered at the Workforce & Technology Center campus in Baltimore.

Ability to climb stairs
Must be able to stand, stoop, bend and stretch for long periods of time
Must be able to do the same jobs many times
Must be able to work alone or with a group
Must be able to measure and mix cleaners
Must be able to lift up to 50 pounds
Must be able to follow verbal and written directions
Must have strong grip strength

structured_extraction.program_name: Food Is Safe Here (FISH) Initiative - Food Safety Training for School Nutrition Professionals (ServSafe)
structured_extraction.program_description: An ongoing program of food safety training options and resources for school food service personnel in Maryland participating in federally funded child nutrition programs. Includes ServSafe Food Handler and Food Manager Training and review sessions using the National Restaurant Association's ServSafe curriculum and certification exam. Training materials are available for school nutrition staff to provide basic food safety instruction. Certified ServSafe Instructors and Proctors from local education agencies can teach classes and order materials at no cost.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Ongoing program providing food safety training options and resources for school food service personnel. Includes ServSafe Food Handler and Food Manager Training and review sessions using the National Restaurant Association's ServSafe curriculum and certification exam. Training materials are available for school nutrition staff to provide basic food safety instruction. Certified ServSafe Instructors and Proctors from local education agencies can teach classes and order materials at no cost. Materials and training are provided at no cost to participating schools.
structured_extraction.program_audience: School nutrition managers, supervisors, directors, and other school nutrition staff and school food service personnel in Maryland participating in federally funded child nutrition programs
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Food safety training, certification, and resources for school nutrition staff
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Maryland
requirements_list: Must be school nutrition personnel or school food service personnel at schools participating in federally funded child nutrition programs
School nutrition managers, supervisors, and directors must receive a minimum of 8 hours of food safety training for USDA Professional Standards
Must be a Certified ServSafe Instructor or Proctor from a local education agency to teach classes or order answer sheets and administer exams
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the online Training Materials Order Form to request ServSafe training materials. Training dates must be scheduled before placing orders. Place orders four weeks in advance to allow for processing and delivery. Certified ServSafe Instructors from local education agencies can teach ServSafe Manager classes. Certified Proctors can order answer sheets and administer certification exams. Contact the Office of School and Community Nutrition Programs at 410-767-0199 for information on additional available training options, resources, and to discuss your school's food safety training needs.

structured_extraction.program_description: A job training program that provides seven weeks of classroom instruction and hands-on experience in food preparation, kitchen operations, and customer service, followed by a seven-week internship at a local business in the food service industry. The program is designed to prepare job seekers with disabilities for jobs in the food service industry, including cafeterias, restaurants, and food stores, and is offered in partnership with the Community College of Baltimore County at the DORS Workforce & Technology Center (WTC) campus in northeast Baltimore.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides seven weeks of classroom instruction at the Workforce Training Center plus hands-on experience in the WTC cafeteria, followed by a seven-week internship at a local business. Training covers food handling and preparation skills, kitchen safety and equipment operation, recipe reading and following, food portions and nutrition, weighing and measuring foods, customer service skills, point of sale skills and register operation, and ServSafe principles.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Job seekers with disabilities seeking training in food service who can meet the program's physical and communication requirements.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Training in food handling, preparation, kitchen safety, customer service, point of sale operations, and ServSafe principles, culminating in paid or unpaid internship experience at local businesses in the food service industry.

Ability to stoop, bend, and stretch
Ability to be considerate and work well with others
Ability to communicate effectively
Ability to follow two-step instructions
Ability to lift and carry 30 pound food containers and trays
Ability to stand for long periods of time

structured_extraction.program_name: Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program (USDA DOD Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program)
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides free fresh fruits and vegetables to children at eligible elementary schools during the school day, promoting nutrition education and healthier school environments. The program also enables Maryland schools to receive weekly deliveries of fresh fruits and vegetables from a Maryland-based produce company, with an emphasis on locally available products, using allocated USDA Foods funds.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Provides free fresh fruits and vegetables to children at participating elementary schools during the school day. Schools can allocate all or a portion of their allocated USDA Foods funds to this program, ordering their choice of fruits and vegetables delivered from a Maryland-based produce company with an emphasis on locally available products. The program introduces children to new varieties of fresh produce and increases overall consumption of fresh, unprocessed produce among young children.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Children attending participating elementary schools across Maryland, including eligible schools and residential child care institutions
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Purchase and provision of fresh fruits and vegetables to students during the school day
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available at participating elementary schools across Maryland (currently 196 schools)
requirements_list: School must be an elementary school
School must participate in the program
School or institution must be eligible per USDA and MSDE guidelines
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Elementary schools participate through the Office of School and Community Nutrition Programs at the Maryland State Department of Education. Applications are accepted annually.
